food.text: By about 1800 BCE, Native Americans in the eastern woodlands were cultivating food plants, beginning a shift from hunting and gathering toward agriculture. Archaeologists now accept that this was one of about ten independent centers of plant domestication in the world.

Starting around 3000 BC, evidence of large-scale oyster harvesting appears in the Southeastern Woodlands. Between 3000 BC and 1000 BC, people built shell rings, large middens surrounding open centers, that are numerous in South Carolina and Georgia.

Chenopodium berlandieri, a plant now widely regarded as a weed, was once a cultivated pseudocereal in North America. By 1700 BC it had clearly been domesticated, and it was grown alongside maygrass, little barley and knotweed as a nutritional basis for Indigenous groups.
Around 3000 BC, the Cochise tradition of the American Southwest began cultivating a primitive form of maize imported from Mesoamerica. Common beans and squash followed later.
The first four plants known to have been domesticated at the Riverton Site in Illinois in 1800 BCE were goosefoot, sunflower, marsh elder and squash. Several other species were domesticated later.

On Horr's Island in Southwest Florida, resources were rich enough to support sizable mound-building communities year-round. Four shell or sand mounds there have been dated to between 2900 and 2300 BC.
Around 3000 BC, people in the American South began cultivating sunflower and marsh elder, while northeastern natives grew amaranth and marsh elder. After harvesting, they ground the seeds into flour.
Around 1600 BC, maize appeared in the Eastern Woodlands. For about 3000 years it remained only a minor part of garden plots, and became a major food only around 1150 AD.

The oldest evidence of maize cultivation north of the Rio Grande dates to about 2100 BCE, at several locations in what later became Arizona and New Mexico. The oldest known maize in Mexico dates to 6700 BCE.
Poverty Point people lived off fishing, gathering and hunting, and their diet changed with the seasons. It included deer, possum, fish, turtles, mollusks, nuts, fruits, berries and aquatic roots.

Archaeologists tell cultivated plants from wild ones by their seeds. Domesticated plants had larger edible seeds and thinner seed coats than wild relatives, a result of human selection. When cultivation later ceased, the seeds reverted to their earlier size and thickness.

The oldest evidence for domesticated goosefoot comes from caches of thin-testa seeds found in rock shelters in the Ozark Plateaus and Ohio River basin. Its domesticated variety is named C. b. ssp. jonesianum.

The Poverty Point culture used stone cooking balls to prepare meals. Scholars believe dozens of them were heated in a bonfire and dropped into pits along with food, and different-shaped balls controlled cooking temperature and time.

Poverty Point people made small baked shapes of loess called Poverty Point Objects. Archaeologists generally conclude they were used for cooking, and experiments showed that in earth ovens they held heat and helped cook food.

Midden remains at Watson Brake show that people relied on fish, shellfish and riverine animals, supplemented by goosefoot, knotweed and possibly marshelder. Over time they ate more deer, turkey, raccoon, opossum, squirrel and rabbits.

art.text: Poverty Point in northeastern Louisiana is a vast earthwork of ridges and mounds built by Indigenous people between 1700 and 1100 BCE. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Archaeologists have suggested it served as a settlement, a trading center, or a ceremonial religious complex.

The Poverty Point culture made high-quality, stylized, carved and polished miniature stone beads. Other early eastern North American cultures rarely used stone for beads, choosing softer shell or bone. The beads depict local animals such as owls, dogs, locusts, and turkey vultures.

In the Great Lakes region, the Old Copper complex is known for widespread copper artifacts, including tools, weapons, and ornamental objects. Artifacts from its sites have been dated from 6500 to 1580 BCE.

Mound A at Poverty Point was built remarkably fast, probably in less than three months. Builders first burned the vegetation, covered the area with silt, and then raised the mound in a single massive effort. It holds about 238,000 cubic meters of fill.
The Poverty Point site had an earthen pyramid 50 feet high and 500 feet long, aligned east to west. It also had a large bird effigy mound measuring 70 feet high and 640 feet across.

Copper Culture State Park in Oconto, Wisconsin, contains an ancient burial ground used by the Old Copper complex between around 4,000 and 2,000 BCE. A 13-year-old boy rediscovered it in June 1952 after unearthing human bones while playing in an old quarry.
Mound A is the second-largest earthen mound by volume in eastern North America. Only Monks Mound at Cahokia, begun around 950 to 1000 CE in present-day Illinois, is bigger.

Excavations at Poverty Point sites have revealed animal effigy figures and hand-molded, baked-clay cooking objects. People also used stone cooking balls, heating dozens in a bonfire and dropping them into pits with food. Different-shaped balls controlled cooking temperature and time.

Watson Brake was built over centuries by a hunter-gatherer society, not by farmers. Its dating in a paper published in 1997 pushed back the date of the oldest known earthwork construction by nearly 2000 years. It showed that such societies could plan and organize large work forces.

A sixth mound at Poverty Point, called Mound F, was discovered only in 2013. It stands about 5 feet tall, and charred wood at its base dates it to after about 1280 BCE. That makes it the last Archaic mound added to the site.

science.text: Native Americans were the first to mine and work the copper of Lake Superior and the Keweenaw Peninsula of northern Michigan, between 5000 BCE and 1200 BCE. They used this copper to produce tools. Archaeological expeditions found copper-producing pits and hammering stones used to work the metal.

The Poverty Point culture built a huge earthwork in present-day Louisiana. The site holds earthen ridges and mounds built between 1700 and 1100 BCE, and it is the largest and most complex Late Archaic earthwork site found in North America.

Researchers have learned that Mound A at Poverty Point was built quickly, probably in less than three months. The vegetation was burned first, between 1450 and 1250 BCE by radiocarbon analysis, and the area was covered with silt. Its 238,000 cubic meters of fill make it the second-largest earthen mound in eastern North America.

Isotopic analysis has provided evidence of copper trading routes throughout North America among native peoples. Native Americans mined native copper on a small scale at the Keweenaw deposits and many other locations.

Deep pits on the western side of the Poverty Point plaza may once have held huge wooden posts that served as calendar markers. Using the sun's shadows, the inhabitants could have predicted the changing of the seasons.
One authority calculated that the Poverty Point earthworks would take more than 1,236,007 cubic feet of basket-loaded soil. That would mean 1,350 adults laboring 70 days a year for three years.

Poverty Point's people used materials such as slate, copper, galena, jasper, quartz and soapstone that came from as far as 620 miles (1,000 km) away. This shows the distant reach of their trading network, which covered much of the eastern United States.

The Poverty Point culture made plummets from heavy iron ore imported from Hot Springs, Arkansas, and used them as weights for fish nets. Points of imported gray Midwestern flint were also found at the site.
People of the Stallings culture on the Savannah River began making pottery around 2888 BC. Pottery making was spreading in South America at the time, but it had not yet reached Mesoamerica.

politics.text: The first mound building was an early marker of political and social complexity among cultures in the eastern part of what is now the United States. Later cultures generally developed hierarchical societies with an elite that commanded hundreds or even thousands of workers to dig up tons of earth with hand tools.

Watson Brake's builders were a hunter-gatherer society, not a farming one. Archaeologists had expected large mound sites to belong to sedentary maize growers with a hierarchical, centralized polity. Instead, these people planned and organized large work forces over centuries.

Poverty Point's main complex covers more than one square mile. Six earthwork crescent ridges were built in a concentric arrangement, interrupted by radial aisles. Evidence of residences extends for about 3 miles along the bank of Bayou Macon.

Mound A at Poverty Point was built quickly, probably in less than three months, in a single massive effort. It holds about 238,000 cubic meters of fill, making it the second-largest earthen mound by volume in eastern North America. Only Monks Mound at Cahokia is larger.

Poverty Point was not built all at once. Its final form appears to be the product of successive generations over a long time. Recent syntheses suggest earthwork construction began as early as 1800 BCE and continued until as late as 1200 BCE.

A sixth mound, called Mound F, was discovered at Poverty Point in 2013, outside the concentric ridges to the northeast. It is about 5 feet tall. A radiocarbon date on charred wood from its base shows it was built after about 1280 BCE, making it the last Archaic mound added to the site.

philosophy.text: The Poverty Point site in Louisiana has earthen ridges and mounds built between 1700 and 1100 BCE. Archaeologists have proposed several possible functions for it, including a settlement, a trading center, and a ceremonial religious complex.

Excavations at Poverty Point turned up crude human figures, which scholars think were used for religious purposes. They were found alongside animal effigy figures, among a wealth of artifacts left by a culture that thrived from about 1730 to 1350 BC.

Mound A at Poverty Point was probably built in less than three months. Its builders first burned the vegetation, between 1450 and 1250 BCE, then covered the area with silt and raised the mound in a single massive effort with no signs of separate construction phases.

Poverty Point's earthen ridges were built between 1700 and 1100 BCE. Archaeologist William Haag interpreted the aisles dividing the ridge sectors as aligned to the solstices, while astronomer Robert Purrington believes the ridges were aligned geometrically rather than astronomically.

At Poverty Point in Louisiana, archaeologist William Haag interpreted the aisles dividing the ridge sectors as aligned to the solstices. Astronomer Robert Purrington believes the ridges were aligned geometrically instead, and the disagreement stems from each choosing a different center for the site.

Researchers have studied Native American religious beliefs for parallels to explain Poverty Point. Gibson believes the ridges were built with their arcs against the west to keep malevolent spirits of evil and death out of the complex.
At Poverty Point, crude human figures are thought to have been used for religious purposes. The site also held a large bird effigy mound, 70 feet high and 640 feet across.

culture.text: Indigenous peoples of North America began practicing farming approximately 4,000 years ago, late in the Archaic period. By then pottery had started to become common, and the small-scale felling of trees had become feasible.

Archaeologists generally place the emergence of the Ancestral Puebloans around the 12th century BCE, during the Early Basketmaker II Era. Their homeland was the Four Corners region, where Utah, Arizona, New Mexico and Colorado meet.

Archaic Indigenous peoples began using fire in a controlled manner. They intentionally burned vegetation to mimic natural fires that cleared forest understories, which made travel easier and helped herbs and berry-producing plants grow.
The Copper Culture State Park in Oconto, northeastern Wisconsin, holds an ancient burial ground. The Old Copper complex culture used it between around 4,000 and 2,000 BCE.

Ancestral Puebloan communities included the kiva, a congregational space used mostly for ceremonies. They lived in a range of structures, including small family pit houses and larger buildings to house clans.

The Copper Culture State Park's burial ground was rediscovered in June 1952 by a 13-year-old boy who unearthed human bones while playing in an old quarry. By July the Wisconsin Archaeological Survey had started the first archaeological dig.
